results.name: digit_set_inrange_nonmatching_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets inside [min-5,max+5] of sets whose >=2 examples all share a final digit, when the target does NOT end in that digit; observed < null means the model over-produces interval/parity generalization and under-weights the "ends in d" rule people adopt for such sets.
results.code:
# name: digit_set_inrange_nonmatching_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for targets inside [min-5,max+5] of sets whose >=2 examples all share a final digit, when the target does NOT end in that digit; observed < null means the model over-produces interval/parity generalization and under-weights the "ends in d" rule people adopt for such sets.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    ld = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 10)
    same = (np.nanmin(ld, axis=1) == np.nanmax(ld, axis=1)) & (n >= 2)
    mask = same & ((t % 10) != np.nanmax(ld, axis=1)) & (t >= lo - 5) & (t <= hi + 5)
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[mask].mean())

results.name: distance_gradient_corr
results.description: Pearson correlation between yes-response and log(1 + distance from target to nearest example); observed more negative than null means people show a steeper numeric-proximity gradient than the model's rules+intervals produce (less negative = model over-produces proximity).
results.code:
# name: distance_gradient_corr
# description: Pearson correlation between yes-response and log(1 + distance from target to nearest example); observed more negative than null means people show a steeper numeric-proximity gradient than the model's rules+intervals produce (less negative = model over-produces proximity).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    x = np.log1p(dist)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if x.std() == 0 or y.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])

results.name: late_minus_early_session_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials in the second half of the session (trial_index >= 225) minus the first half; a nonzero observed vs null (whose mean tracks only stimulus differences) means a within-session drift in response bias (positive = growing liberalness) the stationary model cannot produce.

results.name: yes_rate_far_parity_violating_targets
results.description: Yes-rate among targets that lie >10 outside the example range AND have the opposite parity of an all-same-parity example set; observed > null means the model under-produces baseline/lapse "yes" answers for concept-inconsistent targets (it has no noise term).
results.code:
# name: yes_rate_far_parity_violating_targets
# description: Yes-rate among targets that lie >10 outside the example range AND have the opposite parity of an all-same-parity example set; observed > null means the model under-produces baseline/lapse "yes" answers for concept-inconsistent targets (it has no noise term).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 2)
    allsame = np.nanmin(par, axis=1) == np.nanmax(par, axis=1)
    mask = allsame & ((t % 2) != np.nanmax(par, axis=1)) & ((t < lo - 10) | (t > hi + 10))
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[mask].mean())

results.name: set_size_yes_rate_difference
results.description: Yes-rate on 4-example sets minus yes-rate on 1-2-example sets; observed less negative (closer to 0) than null means the model's size principle over-produces narrowing of generalization with more examples, more negative means it under-produces it.

results.name: lag1_response_dependence
results.description: P(yes | previous trial yes) minus P(yes | previous trial no) over consecutive trials (trial_index step of 1); observed > null means people show sequential perseveration/response autocorrelation that the trial-independent model does not produce.

results.name: above_minus_below_range_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets above the example maximum minus yes-rate for targets below the example minimum; nonzero observed vs null means people generalize asymmetrically in magnitude (positive = more upward generalization) in a way the model's symmetric intervals/rules do not reproduce.
results.code:
# name: above_minus_below_range_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for targets above the example maximum minus yes-rate for targets below the example minimum; nonzero observed vs null means people generalize asymmetrically in magnitude (positive = more upward generalization) in a way the model's symmetric intervals/rules do not reproduce.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).values
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a, b = r[t > hi], r[t < lo]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: yes_rate_inside_range_parity_consistent
results.description: Yes-rate for targets strictly inside [min,max] of an all-same-parity example set whose examples do NOT all share a final digit, with the target sharing that parity; observed < null means the model over-generalizes within the example span (too confident in interval/parity concepts), observed > null means it under-generalizes.
results.code:
# name: yes_rate_inside_range_parity_consistent
# description: Yes-rate for targets strictly inside [min,max] of an all-same-parity example set whose examples do NOT all share a final digit, with the target sharing that parity; observed < null means the model over-generalizes within the example span (too confident in interval/parity concepts), observed > null means it under-generalizes.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 2)
    ld = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 10)
    digit_same = np.nanmin(ld, axis=1) == np.nanmax(ld, axis=1)
    allsame = np.nanmin(par, axis=1) == np.nanmax(par, axis=1)
    mask = allsame & ~digit_same & ((t % 2) == np.nanmax(par, axis=1)) & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[mask].mean())
